title: London cop's jail sentence in custody death lauded by victim's kin, decried by fellow officers
subtitle: A judge sentenced a London police officer convicted in the 2016 custody death on an Indigenous woman to 12 months in jail Monday, drawing praise from her family and criticism from the police union.
article: A judge sentenced a London police officer convicted in the 2016 custody death of an Indigenous woman to 12 months in jail Monday, drawing praise from her family and criticism from the police union.

Const. Nicholas Doering was found guilty last November of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life in the Sept. 7, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn, marking the first time a Canadian police officer has been convicted of those on-duty crimes.

Doering, 30, arrested Chrisjohn, 39, after she was found trying to get into vehicles in east London while high on crystal meth. He transferred the mother of 11 into OPP custody on an outstanding warrant, falsely telling two officers that she'd been medically cleared, court heard.

Justice Renee Pomerance rejected the defence's push for a conditional sentence that would include probation and community service, saying nothing short of a jail term would reflect the gravity of the offences committed.
"The message conveyed by a conditional sentence would be the wrong message," said Pomerance, who read her sentencing decision during an hour-long conference call.

"Const. Doering demonstrated a wanton and reckless disregard for Ms. Chrisjohn's life. He failed to obtain the necessary medical treatment. He ignored the gross deterioration of her condition and he lied about her condition to the OPP, making it even less likely that her life would be saved."
Chrisjohn's sister, Cindy, said the family has been waiting for Monday's sentencing decision for four years.
"The judge was very clear that he must go to jail for lying to other police about her medical situation and for not treating her like she was a human being. We support that," she said in a statement.
Doering was ordered to surrender himself to custody within 24 hours.
But he filed an appeal and was released on bail, his appeal lawyer, Alan Gold, confirmed through an assistant.
A jail sentence would result in Doering's dismissal, but his appeal keeps him on the police payroll as the case works its way through the courts.
Doering, who had been assigned to administrative duties since he was charged, was suspended with pay Monday, police Chief Steve Williams said in a statement.

"I am aware of Const. Doering's sentence today and have reviewed the decision. The circumstances of this case are tragic and difficult for everyone involved," Williams said, adding police will launch an internal probe once the criminal case is complete.

During Doering's trial, the court heard how London police had arrested Chrisjohn the day before her death, when she was also high on crystal meth, but left her at hospital after the OPP, who had an outstanding warrant for her arrest, declined to pick her up until she was cleared medically.

Doering arrested her the next day, but didn't ask paramedics at the scene to assess her. Chrisjohn was lying handcuffed in the backseat of Doering's cruiser, shaking and moaning as he drove her to a south-end parking lot, where he told two OPP officers that she'd been in the same unresponsive state since he picked her up, but had been medically cleared, the court heard.

St. Thomas paramedics were called later to the Elgin OPP detachment, where they found a motionless Chrisjohn lying on the floor of her cell, breathing irregularly. She died at the hospital from cardiac arrest connected to crystal meth use, the court heard.

Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, announced charges against Doering and OPP Const. Mark McKillop in July 2017. Charges against McKillop, who testified at Doering's trial, were withdrawn later.
Doering's stereotypes and assumptions about drug users played a role in Chrisjohn's death, Pomerance said, but no evidence suggested her Indigenous status influenced his actions.

"Ms. Chrisjohn died in police custody because she was not provided with the most basic level of care," she said. "This has the potential to reinforce the belief among indigenous peoples that police are not their protectors, rather persons to be protected from."

Pomerance said she accepted that Doering, who has apologized publicly to Chrisjohn's family twice, is remorseful and his crimes weren't premeditated, but he had turned a blind eye to risks that would have been apparent to any "reasonably prudent" police officer.
Doering has no previous criminal record and has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, both factors that were taken into consideration for his sentencing.
Growing up in the Woodstock area, Doering became a London police cadet in 2009 and was hired as a constable two years later.

London Police Association took aim at Pomerance's sentencing, saying it "sets an unsustainable precedent and establishes an exacting standard of care in a system that already pushes our law enforcement personnel to their limits."

"We believe that if this decision stands, it will be both counterproductive and inhibiting in relation to officers that find themselves in similar difficult situations," the union said in a statement.
The association expressed sympathy to the Chrisjohn family and highlighted the need to address drug addiction in the community.

"Continuing the current health-care and policing model, whereby police officers are held accountable for systematic inadequacies in health care, addiction and mental health response, will only lead to further tragedy," the union said.

Cindy Chrisjohn was critical of the association's statement, saying, "We were sure that after Nicholas Doering was convicted and sentenced that the London police would finally see the harm that his actions caused."

Pomerance said her sentence wasn't meant to put a value on the life of Chrisjohn, described by family as a loving matriarch whose struggles with addiction didn't stop her from providing her children with affection, a sense of belonging and a connection to their Indigenous ancestry.

"Const. Doering has to live with the knowledge that his actions led to the death of another human being. That reality is likely more punishing than any sentence this court could ever impose," Pomerance said.
